items.title: A writer from scratch
items.prose: Put the level together in one function: count, turn to chances, apply the temperature and sample. `power` is 1, 2 (temperature $\tfrac12$) or 0.5 (temperature 2). Use the rule from the lessons: the first word whose running total is above `u`, else the last word.
items.question: Write `bigram_writer(text, start, us, power)`: return the words written from `start`, one per `u`, stopping early at a word that starts no pair.

widget.starter:
def bigram_writer(text, start, us, power):
    # 1. count the pairs of the text, keeping next words in order of first appearance
    # 2. for each u: take the row of the word now, raise its counts to power,
    #    rescale, and pick the first word whose running total is above u
    # 3. stop early if the word now starts no pair
    return [start]
widget.solution:
def bigram_writer(text, start, us, power):
    words = text.split()
    heads = []
    nexts = []
    counts = []
    for i in range(len(words) - 1):
        a = words[i]
        b = words[i + 1]
        if a not in heads:
            heads.append(a)
            nexts.append([])
            counts.append([])
        k = heads.index(a)
        if b in nexts[k]:
            counts[k][nexts[k].index(b)] += 1
        else:
            nexts[k].append(b)
            counts[k].append(1)
    out = [start]
    word = start
    for u in us:
        if word not in heads:
            break
        k = heads.index(word)
        raised = []
        for c in counts[k]:
            raised.append(c ** power)
        total = 0
        for r in raised:
            total = total + r
        chosen = nexts[k][-1]
        running = 0
        for j in range(len(raised)):
            running = running + raised[j] / total
            if u < running:
                chosen = nexts[k][j]
                break
        word = chosen
        out.append(word)
    return out

explain.text: Build the rows in first-seen order, raise each count to `power` and divide by their total, then walk the running totals. Raising counts or chances to the same power gives the same rescaled row, because the row total cancels.

items.title: From text to sentence
items.prose: You want a script that writes a new sentence from a text.
items.question: Put the steps in order and leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Split the text into words, counting each full stop as a word
Count every pair of neighbouring words into a next-word table
Divide each count by its row total to get chances
Apply the temperature: raise each chance to a power and rescale
Start at a word and draw a random $u$ from 0 to 1
Take the first next word whose running total is above $u$, then repeat from it
Divide each count by the number of words in the text

feedback.correct: Split, count, divide, temperature, draw, walk.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Chances need counts, and sampling needs chances.

byKey.bad: Dividing by the words in the text gives a row that does not add to 1. Divide by the row total.
byKey.temp: The temperature reshapes chances, so the chances must come first.

explain.text: Counts come from the pairs, chances from the counts, and the temperature reshapes the chances. Only then does each random $u$ pick a word from the running totals.

items.question: What is the first word's chance at temperature $\tfrac12$? Give a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn counts into chances, square, then rescale.

byKey.no-rescale: $\tfrac14$ is the square of $\tfrac12$. Rescale by the total of the squares, $\tfrac38$.
byKey.same: $\tfrac12$ is the chance at temperature 1. Square and rescale.

explain.text: The chances are $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac14$, and their squares $\tfrac14, \tfrac1{16}, \tfrac1{16}$ add to $\tfrac38$. So the first word gets $\tfrac14 \div \tfrac38 = \tfrac23$.

items.prose: A picker is written with `u <= total` instead of `u < total`. On the row for “the” (cat $\tfrac12$, mat, jam and dog $\tfrac16$ each) it gets $u = 0.5$ and writes cat.
items.question: Which word does the lessons' rule give for $u = 0.5$, and why?

options.text: mat: 0.5 is not above $\tfrac12$, so walk on

options.why: The rule needs a running total above $u$. Equal is not above, so 0.5 goes to mat.

options.text: Either: one draw of exactly 0.5 never matters
options.why: Such a draw is rare, but a picker must follow one rule exactly, or its runs stop matching the tests and other seeded runs.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the rule: above $u$.

explain.text: cat's piece runs from 0 up to, but not including, $\tfrac12$. With `u < total`, 0.5 walks on to mat, whose running total $\tfrac23$ is above it.

items.title: Fluent nonsense
items.prompt:
A next-word table trained on news text writes: “the bank cut rates rose sharply on the bank cut rates”. Each pair of words reads well, but the sentence makes no sense.

(a) Say what the table knows when it picks a word. (b) Explain why every pair reads well. (c) Explain why the whole sentence can still be nonsense, with one example from the course text. (d) Say what a model would need to do better, and what temperature can and cannot fix.
items.model:
**(a)** The table knows one thing when it picks: the word just written. It looks up that word's row and picks the next word by its chance. It keeps no memory of anything earlier.

**(b)** Every pair it writes was counted in real text. “bank cut”, “cut rates” and “rates rose” each appeared in the news. So each neighbouring pair is a pair someone wrote.

**(c)** Meaning needs more than pairs. “rates rose” is fine after “interest”, but after “the bank cut rates” it contradicts what came before, and the table cannot see that far back. In the course text, “the cat ate the cat sat on the mat” is built from real pairs, yet no one wrote it and it makes little sense.

**(d)** A better model must look further back: at many earlier words, not one. Real chatbots use networks that read a long run of tokens before choosing. Temperature cannot fix it: it only sharpens or flattens the same row. A temperature near 0 repeats the likeliest pairs, as in “the cat sat on the cat sat on”; a high one makes rarer pairs more likely. Neither adds memory.

rubric.text: States that the table conditions only on the last word
Explains that every written pair was seen in the training text
Explains why pairs can join into nonsense, with a concrete example
Says a better model must use more context (more earlier tokens)
Says temperature only reshapes one row's chances and cannot add memory
